Over 4 years since COVID-19 emerged and despite rapid vaccine development, 1 the long-term pandemic mortality impact and its determining factors remain only partially understood. 2

Calculating excess all-cause mortality by comparing observed and expected deaths during a specified time period 3 provides valuable insights into the direct and indirect impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, including mortality associated with overwhelmed healthcare systems and other pandemic adverse effects. 3 While many studies have focused on specific countries or regions to examine excess mortality, 4–7 they often relied on provisional public data, the consistency of which was affected by the frequency of updates. 8 , 9

Understanding how government responses and vaccination efforts influenced the global pandemic toll is crucial. 1 , 10 Vaccines have played a pivotal role in reducing COVID-19 mortality and preventing healthcare system overload by decreasing infections and severe cases. 11–13 However, overwhelmed healthcare systems and strict measures reduced healthcare access and worsened health outcomes, while pandemic-related lifestyle and mental health implications possibly contributed to excess deaths during and after the pandemic. 14 Further, a study of 31 European countries found that those with successful protective measures during the pandemic experienced higher mortality rates after restrictions were lifted—a phenomenon termed the reverse harvesting effect. 15 The widespread relaxation of restrictions, economic reopening, and increased vaccination rates in 2022 altered healthcare systems, thus affecting excess-mortality patterns and warranting close examination of this period.

Building on previous estimates of excess all-cause mortality in 24 countries for 2020–1, 10 this study examines excess mortality in 2022 (total, sex-specific, and age-specific) by analysing weekly mortality data across 2020–2 from 21 C-MOR consortium countries. 8 , 16 We also analysed the relationship between government control measures, with a focus on vaccination, and excess mortality during 2021–2. These findings aim to aid policymakers in addressing ongoing healthcare challenges from the COVID-19 pandemic and in improving responses to similar future public health emergencies.
### Data acquisition

Data availability was the sole criterion for inclusion in the study and 21 C-MOR consortium countries and/or regions provided mortality data for this ecological study. The participating countries or regions were Australia, Austria, Brazil, Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark, England and Wales, Estonia, France, Georgia, Greece, Israel, Italy, Mauritius, Northern Ireland, Norway, Peru, Poland, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, and the USA. Total, sex-specific, and age-specific weekly all-cause mortality data for 2015–22 were obtained from national vital statistics databases ( Supplementary Table S1 ). Data were compiled in mid-2023 to account for reporting delays 9 , 17 and allow reporting authorities sufficient time to consolidate and enhance the quality of the data. 18

Moreover, weekly COVID-19 deaths were obtained for each country for all three of the years of 2020–2 from national vital statistics databases. For the countries that were unable to provide COVID-19 deaths, data were acquired from the online database “Our World In Data.” 19

Data on total vaccinations by manufacturer for each country in 2021 and 2022 were obtained from “Our World In Data.” 19 Vaccine doses per 100 000 population, including primary and booster doses, were calculated weekly. For other infection control measures, data on eight governmental policy measures under “Closure and Containment” were sourced from the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker. 20 These measures were ordinal categorical variables, with weekly values estimated as the mode of daily indicators. Additionally, the weekly average stringency index of government measures 20 and COVID-19 incidence per 100 000 population were analysed for their association with excess mortality. Descriptions and sources of these variables are available in Supplementary Tables S2 and S3 .

### Statistical analysis

The same methodology as previously used 10 was employed for calculating mortality rates and estimating excess mortality,. Crude mortality rates (CMRs) were first calculated for the total population and sex-specific by using population estimates from the World Bank, 21 the UK Office for National Statistics, 22 and Eurostat. 23 Age-specific mortality rates (ASpMRs) and weekly (directly) age-standardized mortality rates (ASMRs) were then calculated by using the aggregated age groups provided by each country. These age groups are detailed in Supplementary Table S4 followed by the equations used for the calculation of CMRs, ASpMRs, and ASMRs.

Total and sex-specific weekly excess mortality for 2022 was calculated by comparing the observed weekly 2022 ASMR (per 100 000 population) against the expected weekly ASMR in 2022, estimated based on a time-series regression analysis of historical data (2015– 19) as previously described. 8 , 10 , 24–26 Likewise, age-specific weekly excess mortality for 2022 was calculated by comparing the observed weekly 2022 CMR (per 100 000 population) against the expected weekly CMR in 2022, estimated based on historical data (2015–19).

The regression models were built on complete weeks; truncated weeks—usually as a result of the different death counts observed around Christmas and New Year 27 —were excluded, as shown in Supplementary Table S5 . Sex-specific excess mortality for 2022 could not be calculated for Northern Ireland due to the lack of sex-specific all-cause mortality data and thus Northern Ireland was not included in this analysis. Also, sex-specific weekly all-cause mortality for Peru was collected from 2017 to 2022.

The weekly comparison of observed and expected mortality rates is visually depicted by using z-scores. Z-scores ranging from −2 to +2 are considered “normal,” whereas a z-score of >4 is considered a substantial increase. 28 , 29

To estimate the excess mortality for 2022, the cumulative expected mortality rate was subtracted from the observed rate. By using a time-series regression model, 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. The 95% CIs were also estimated by using the time-series regression model. The P-score—defined as the ratio of the cumulative excess to the cumulative expected mortality, expressed as a percentage—was calculated for 2022, for the total population, by sex, and for age groups <65, 65+, <70 and 70+years.

To understand the relationship between the weekly number of vaccine doses (primary and booster), governmental control measures, and weekly excess mortality, multilevel models were employed, as detailed in the Supplementary Methods .

All analyses were performed by using R Statistical Software, version 2024.04.2 + 764 (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
### Weekly comparisons—total population and by sex and age group in 2020–2

Weekly excess-mortality results between 2020 and 2022 are presented in the Supplementary Results section, Supplementary Figures S2–S5 , and Supplementary Table S6 . Briefly, in 2022, all countries showed a substantial increase in the ASMR for the total population, ranging from 1 to 10 weeks. The excess-mortality duration among the countries varied between 1–12 weeks and between 1 and 8 weeks, for males and females, respectively. Lastly, excess mortality was higher in the older age groups investigated (65+ and 70+years).

### Cumulative excess mortality in 2022

Figure 1 illustrates the cumulative excess all-cause mortality for 2020, 2021, and 2022. Supplementary Table S7 shows the cumulative observed and expected all-cause ASMRs for 2022, while Supplementary Table S8 shows the difference between the cumulative observed and expected all-cause ASMRs for 2020 and 2021. Supplementary Table S9 provides data for all three of the years 2020, 2021, and 2022 combined. It is important to note that countries report aggregated mortality data in different age groups, so calculated ASMRs are not directly comparable.

All participating countries presented substantial excess cumulative mortality in 2022. Notably, Australia, Austria, Cyprus, Denmark, Israel, Italy, Norway, Spain, and Sweden experienced a higher excess mortality in 2022 than in 2021, whereas Australia, Cyprus, Denmark, Israel, Mauritius, and Norway experienced the highest excess mortality in 2022. Additionally, all countries except Mauritius demonstrated a substantial increase in yearly all-cause mortality across the 3 years combined.

Supplementary Table S10 details the yearly cumulative mortality rate differences by sex for 2022. In 2022, all countries showed significant excess cumulative mortality for both males and females. Figure 2 (2021 and 2022) and Supplementary Table S11 show the male-to-female cumulative excess ASMR ratios. Generally, males were more affected, with females being more affected than males in Cyprus in 2022 and in Australia, Denmark, and Mauritius in 2021.

Supplementary Table S12 demonstrates the cumulative CMR differences (observed–expected) by age group for the year 2022. Age-specific excess all-cause mortality was higher in the older age groups of 65+ and 70+years than in those in the younger age groups for both years.

Figure 3 and Supplementary Table S13 illustrate variations in the reporting and categorization of COVID-19 deaths and overall crude mortality. Despite the total number of deaths appearing similar across the 3 years (2020–2), in some countries, there was a noticeable increase in reported COVID-19 deaths in 2021 with a simultaneous decrease in non-COVID-19 deaths during the same year, suggesting a possible overdetection of cases and overreporting of deaths as COVID-19 deaths. This is not surprising given the test availability and meticulous testing procedures, particularly in hospitals, which increased the likelihood of COVID-19 detection and deaths being coded as COVID-19 deaths. Additionally, the data indicate that, in many countries, non-COVID-19 death rates returned to or surpassed the 2020 levels in 2022, which may reflect changes in detection and reporting practices during 2022.

### Impact of vaccination and other governmental policies on excess mortality

We developed year-specific multilevel models to examine the influence of total vaccinations on excess mortality. These models also examined the weekly incidence of reported COVID-19 cases, overall stringency of governmental control measures, and weekly non-COVID-19 mortality. The random-effect estimates for each country introduced variation in the model, with intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.63 for 2021 and 0.55 for 2022. In both mixed models, non-COVID-19 mortality was most strongly associated with excess mortality, negatively for 2021 ( β 2021 = –2.21, P < 0.001) and positively for 2022( β 2022 = 1.24, P < 0.001). Total vaccinations per 100 population were independently negatively associated with excess mortality in 2022 ( β 2022 = –0.49, P = 0.005). The stringency of control measures was negatively associated with excess mortality in 2021, but weakly positively in 2022 ( β 2021 = –0.62, P < 0.001, and β 2022 = 0.16, P = 0.031) ( Table 1 ).

Supplementary Figures S6–10 and Supplementary Table S14 with its description show the results of regression analyses to examine the relationship between the number of vaccine doses administered and excess mortality, for various vaccines, in the years 2021 and 2022. Briefly, only Pfizer/BioNTech (2021: β = –0.00200, P < 0.001 and 2022: β = –0.00162, P < 0.001) and Moderna (2021: β = –0.00326, P = 0.023 and 2022: β = –0.00152, P = 0.0778) vaccines showed negative relationships with cumulative excess mortality in both 2021 and 2022.

With respect to governmental policies, Supplementary Figures S11–S18 show the percentage of weeks in each year (2020–2) for which a specific stringency level of each policy was applied in each country. For most policies, higher stringency levels were more common in previous years than in 2022.

The relationship between each governmental policy measure (3-week lag) and excess mortality, accounting for total vaccinations and non-COVID-19 mortality, are shown in Figure 4 (unadjusted models are presented in Supplementary Figure S19 ). In 2021, all policy measures—with the exception of the strictest levels of school closing, restrictions on gatherings, closing of public transport, and stay-at-home requirements—were negatively associated with excess mortality. On the other hand, in 2022, most measures were positively associated with excess mortality, with the exception of the lowest stringency levels for school closing, public transport closing, and international travel controls.
Ethics approval to conduct the study was obtained from the Cyprus National Bioethics Committee (16/6/2020, ΕΕΒΚ/ΕΠ/2020/01.127).
question: Based on the statistical analysis of antigen-specific immune response triggered by biological agents derived from weakened or killed pathogens that stimulate immune recognition without causing disease and its effects on population-level disease distribution across multiple countries, what can be inferred about the role of this intervention in influencing excess mortality during 2022?

choices.Option: The reversal in the association between governmental control measures and excess mortality from 2021 to 2022 may reflect the increased virulence of the Omicron variant, which reduced the effectiveness of public health interventions despite high vaccination rates.

The negative association between total vaccinations and excess mortality in 2022 may be due to increased reporting of non-COVID-19 deaths in countries with higher vaccination rates, rather than a true protective effect of vaccines.
In 2022, the mitigating effect of total vaccinations on excess mortality was evident at both the weekly level and the yearly cumulative level across countries.

The strong, negative, significant correlation between vaccination rates and the stringency index in 2021 (r = –0.6719; P < 0.0001) suggests that higher vaccination coverage led to the relaxation of control measures, potentially offsetting the benefits of vaccination in reducing excess mortality.

The lack of a significant mitigating effect of vaccination on excess mortality in 2021, despite high mRNA vaccine coverage, suggests that vaccination campaigns were ineffective in reducing severe outcomes during that year.

Clubfoot prevalence in the Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population (hereafter respectfully Indigenous) is higher than global estimates. 1–3 In the Northern Territory (NT), where clubfoot prevalence has not been formally reported, Indigenous people comprise 30% of the population compared with 4% Australia-wide. 4 Strong cultural practices serve as a protective force for Indigenous families, with cultural determinants of health fostering resilience despite challenges across health, English-based education, employment, and housing. 5 , 6 Understanding clubfoot prevalence in the NT, particularly among Indigenous families, will inform service priorities and research in line with Indigenous perspectives and cultural values.

Clubfoot, or congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), is the most common congenital orthopaedic condition worldwide, affecting an estimated 176 000 births annually, with males typically affected twice as often as females. 3 , 7 The majority (75%–85%) of clubfoot is isolated (i.e. without an identifiable comorbid condition or syndrome at birth) and is characterized by stiffness in ankle equinus, hindfoot varus, cavus, and adductus of the forefoot. 7–9 Bilateral clubfoot is typically more severe and more common than unilateral cases, and the features of left and right feet are correlated. 10 Although the aetiology of clubfoot is unknown, multifactorial (genetic and environmental) factors appear involved. 7 Unlike positional talipes, which presents similarly but is flexible and resolves soon after birth, 11 untreated clubfoot leads to disability. 12 Further investigation of clubfoot characteristics and the prevalence in Australia is required.

Globally, clubfoot prevalence is 1.18/1000 births. 3 In Australia, isolated clubfoot prevalence has been investigated in only two regions. In Western Australian (WA), the prevalence was 1.25/1000 in the general population compared with 3.49/1000 for babies born to Indigenous mothers 1 and Indigenous maternity was a risk factor [odds ratio (OR) 2.82]. 13 In South Australia (SA), the prevalence was 1.1/1000, with an Indigenous maternity risk factor (OR 2.0). 2 Anecdotal evidence from NT clinicians who manage clubfoot is consistent with these studies, suggesting over-representation of Indigenous Australians and the need to formally evaluate clubfoot in the NT.

There is limited Australian literature about clubfoot prevalence and formal studies in the NT are lacking. To establish the extent of isolated clubfoot in the NT, the aim of this study was to enumerate and then describe the characteristics of babies with isolated clubfoot. This permitted the first reliable estimate of the birth prevalence of isolated clubfoot for the NT.
### Study design

We conducted a retrospective study under the stewardship of a senior Indigenous community leader, researcher, and health professional (S.T.).

### Setting

The NT is a unique geographical and cultural region of Australia. Covering 1.3 million km 2 , this sparsely populated region encompasses 17% of Australia’s land mass, yet is home to just 1% of the population. 14 , 15 Of nearly 250 000 people, the NT population includes ∼75 000 Indigenous people (30% compared with 4% nationally), who mostly live in remote or very remote areas (73% compared with 15% nationally). 4 , 15 Remoteness limits access to health services. Remote primary health clinics operated by Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations (ACCHOs) and NT Health (the NT government-funded health service) provide essential care, yet many people, including those with clubfoot, must travel hundreds of kilometres by road, air, or sea to larger centres for specialist care.

Established clinical practice in the NT is that, at birth, babies with clubfoot are referred to NT Health clubfoot physiotherapists to coordinate care. Almost all births (97%) in the NT occur in hospitals and all births have routine screening by medical professionals at the earliest opportunity. 16 Of six hospitals with birthing services, only the two largest NT Health-operated centres provide clubfoot services. Expert physiotherapist assessment is provided at birth in those hospitals or via telehealth with subsequent travel to a larger centre for further management. The gold-standard Ponseti method is standard care, involving initial correction via serial plaster casts and Achilles tenotomy, then maintenance via long-term bracing. 17

### Sources

We examined clinical records of all babies born with clubfoot in the NT during the 14-year period from 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2022. Several sources of information were examined to ascertain potential cases of isolated clubfoot:

Data from all sources were merged and duplicates removed. Potential cases underwent desktop audit, reviewing available electronic information such as birth admission, discharge summary, letters, operation records, and non-hospital clinic records. A full primary hardcopy medical record audit was undertaken if it was impossible to exclude isolated clubfoot via desktop audit or to differentiate between isolated clubfoot, positional talipes, syndromic clubfoot, and other foot presentations.

### Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Isolated clubfoot was defined as a foot with fixed plantarflexion, supination, and adduction in the absence of any known congenital condition or syndrome in the neonatal period. 9 Babies were candidates for the analysis if born to NT residents with a documented diagnosis of clubfoot (confirmed by orthopaedic, paediatric, or physiotherapy consultation) or a sufficient description of the foot that met this definition. Other foot and toe deformities were excluded. Where ‘talipes’ was recorded in the NTMC yet neither electronic nor full hardcopy records revealed evidence of any foot condition, the case was taken to be transient positional talipes and excluded. Interstate births to NT residents were included if the birth history was available within NT records.

### Data compilation, management, and storage

After ascertainment, a custom data-extraction tool was applied to all electronic and hardcopy records of confirmed cases ( Supplementary Material ). The tool, data-collection guide, and protocol were developed a priori by K.P. (senior physiotherapist), R.B. (physiotherapy researcher), and A.C. (epidemiologist). REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture) 19 , 20 was used to record and secure demographic, obstetric, and birth information; clinical measures; outcomes; and events. Clubfoot clinical outcomes will be presented in a separate study. Additional maternal data not available in the medical records of infants were sourced from the NTPR.

### Variables

Variables used to describe infant characteristics ( Supplementary Table S1 ) included sex, birthweight, gestational age, length, head circumference, laterality of clubfoot, and family history of clubfoot. The severity of clubfoot, indicated by the earliest Pirani score, was also recorded. 21 Variables used to describe maternal factors ( Supplementary Table S1 ) included mother’s age, remoteness index [Modified Monash Model (MMM)], 22 distance from home to treatment centre, diabetes status, body mass index (BMI), birth parity, birth presentation, and smoking or alcohol use during pregnancy.

### Data analysis

The birth prevalence [/1000 live births, 95% confidence interval (CI)] was calculated by following established methods using the isolated clubfoot cases as the numerator and all live births in the NT during the observation period as the denominator. 23 Denominator data were obtained from the NTPR of all live births in the NT by year, ethnicity, and sex. Information was not sourced for fetal deaths or terminations.

Characteristics of Indigenous babies with clubfoot were compared with characteristics of non-Indigenous babies with clubfoot by using IBM SPSS. 24 For categorical variables, ORs and 95% CIs were calculated by using binary logistic regression. For numeric variables, comparisons were made by using independent t -tests or Mann–Whitney U tests for normally and non-normally distributed data, respectively.
### Case identification

Sources were combined to identify cases of isolated clubfoot in the NT ( Fig. 1 ). Physiotherapy case-management databases contained 191 potential cases, the NTMC contained 152 potential cases, and ICD-10-AM coding data contained 1222 potential cases. After duplicates were removed, 1051 records were screened. Desktop audit excluded 277 cases, then 774 underwent full medical record audit. This confirmed 150 babies with isolated clubfoot in the observation period ( Fig. 1 ).

Clubfoot diagnosis was not easily confirmed within the NTMC or coding sources due to the use of ambiguous terminology and umbrella codes. Within the NTMC, the term ‘talipes’ was the most common label used (57%), but was applied to both clubfoot and positional talipes (45% and 40% of uses, respectively). ‘Clubfoot’ was used infrequently, although usually (92%) correctly ( Supplementary Table S2A ). Within the coding data, seven different ICD-10-AM codes were used for isolated clubfoot cases. Umbrella codes, which include but are not exclusive to clubfoot, were used most (50% of codes overall), with 24% of umbrella codes applied to cases of clubfoot and 64% to positional talipes. The single specific clubfoot code for both isolated and syndromic cases was used for 9% of clubfoot cases ( Supplementary Table S2B ). The non-specific terminology within the NTMC and the use of umbrella ICD-10-AM codes meant that neither source alone could accurately ascertain all cases of isolated clubfoot.

### Characteristics of clubfoot cases

Among 150 babies with isolated clubfoot (hereafter ‘clubfoot’), 109 (73%) were Indigenous, 113 (75%) were male, 85 (57%) were unilateral cases [of them, 49 (58%) right-sided], and the gestational age ranged from 30 to 41 weeks (median: 39 weeks), including 25 (17%) preterm babies. The mean maternal age was 27 years (range: 13–44 years, SD: 6.1 years), 49 (33%) babies were the mother’s firstborn, 11 (7%) were breech at delivery, and 31 (21%) had a first- or second-degree relative with clubfoot. Most (73%) were from remote or very remote areas, with a mean direct distance from home to clubfoot management of 222 km ( Table 1 ).

### Prevalence

During the study period, 53 591 live births were recorded. For 150 clubfoot cases, the overall birth prevalence for the period was 2.80/1000 (95% CI: 2.38–3.27). The prevalence was five times higher for Indigenous (5.99/1000, 95% CI: 4.95–7.20) compared with non-Indigenous (1.16/1000, 95% CI: 0.84–1.56) babies. The prevalence in males compared with females was 3 times greater, 1.5 times greater for non-Indigenous males, and 4 times greater for Indigenous males. The subgroup prevalence is detailed in Table 2 . No trend in the numbers of clubfoot births over the observation period was evident ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ).

### Comparison of Indigenous with non-Indigenous babies

Indigenous babies with clubfoot compared with non-Indigenous babies with clubfoot were more likely to be male (OR = 2.68; 95% CI: 1.22–5.90; P = 0.014), live in remote or very remote areas (OR = 14.24; CI: 5.98–33.90; P < 0.001), and have younger mothers (OR = 13.88, 95% CI: 3.90–49.39; P < 0.001). Mothers of Indigenous babies with clubfoot were younger [mean age = 25 years (SD = 5.8 years) and 30 years (SD = 5.7 years), respectively; |t|(148) = 4.42; P < 0.001)] and more likely to report smoking (OR = 17.41; 95% CI: 3.93–77.08; P < 0.001) or alcohol use (OR = 4.63; 95% CI: 1.03–20.89; P = 0.046) during pregnancy. No differences were found between groups for birthweight, gestational age, birth length, head circumference, bilateral/unilateral clubfoot, maternal diabetes, BMI, firstborn, breech presentation, or family history ( Table 1 ).

### Severity

No difference in the severity of clubfoot between Indigenous and non-Indigenous groups was seen. The median Pirani score for all 215 feet was 5.0 overall and for both subgroups. The Pirani score ranged from 1.0 to 6.0 for non-Indigenous and 1.5 to 6.0 for Indigenous babies, and, in both groups, ∼60% scored ≥5.0 ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). No difference in severity between the feet of babies with bilateral clubfoot was seen (Related Samples Sign Test P = 0.648). 25 , 26
The Human Research Ethics Committee of NT Health and Menzies School of Health Research provided approval (HREC 2021-3989).
question: What key methodological insight emerges from the study's approach to identifying a rare congenital foot malformation featuring forefoot adduction, midfoot abduction, and hindfoot valgus with structural misalignment at birth in the Northern Territory?

choices.Option: The high prevalence of clubfoot among Indigenous babies in the NT reflects a strong genetic predisposition that is more common in this population compared to non-Indigenous groups.
The study's findings suggest that maternal smoking and alcohol use during pregnancy are direct causes of clubfoot in Indigenous infants.
The use of telehealth for initial clubfoot assessment in remote areas has significantly reduced the need for long-distance travel to specialist centres.
The use of umbrella ICD-10-AM codes and non-specific diagnostic terminology in medical records can lead to inaccurate clubfoot prevalence estimates when relying on single-source data.
The study's ascertainment process was unnecessary because the NTMC and ICD-10-AM coding systems are inherently accurate and reliable for identifying clubfoot cases.

Preterm birth (PTB)—delivery before 37 completed weeks of gestation, with a global prevalence of 10.6%—is the leading cause of death in children who are <5 years old [ 1 ]. This condition is also a common reason for newborn hospital admissions due to severe complications and is associated with poor health in childhood and adulthood [ 2 ].

Tens of studies report associations of ambient temperature with PTB by using various epidemiological study designs, exposure measures, and exposure periods. Most of these studies have examined short-term exposures only. For example, several time series studies found that immediate exposure to high temperature on the day of birth or a few days before is associated with PTB [ 3–7 ]. Similarly, a handful of case-crossover studies observed that exposure to heat during the week before birth is related to PTB [ 8–11 ]. In addition, several cohort studies reported positive associations between high temperatures or heatwaves in the week before birth and PTB [ 12–18 ]. While this literature generally demonstrates positive associations for acute exposures, its main limitation is the lack of consideration of effects in earlier gestation weeks.

Other cohort studies have examined longer-term exposures, such as the last month before birth, the entire pregnancy average, and trimester-specific exposures [ 19–26 ]. Most of these studies fitted separate models for each exposure period. However, as temperatures in different periods during pregnancy are highly correlated, exposure in one period might confound the association between exposure in another period and PTB [ 27 ].

Distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) add different exposure periods (lags) to the model while addressing their collinearity by using a lag–response function [ 28 ]. To date, only three cohort studies have examined associations between temperature and PTB by using DLNMs and survival analysis [ 29–31 ]. Adapting DLNMs to prenatal exposures creates a challenge due to varying gestational lengths. A study in France used two exposure periods in a DLNM: the last 30 days of pregnancy and 26 weeks after conception, to avoid this issue [ 29 ]. While innovative, this approach mixes the reference times of the exposure, as some exposures are defined by gestation week, while other exposures in the same model are determined by the birth date. Moreover, some of these exposure periods overlap for some of the pregnancies. This limits the interpretation of critical periods by gestation weeks. A study in Sweden defined exposure weeks backward from the week of birth, which leads to a similar limitation [ 30 ].

DLNMs can also estimate associations of cumulative exposures throughout pregnancy, calculated for scenarios of fixed exposure relative to another fixed reference exposure. However, such scenarios are unrealistic for most climates, in which temperatures vary throughout pregnancy due to seasonality.

Few studies also examined the effect modification by socioeconomic status (SES) [ 3 , 7 , 11 , 14 , 17 , 22 ], race [ 4 , 8 ], or body mass index (BMI) [ 8 , 32 ], with inconsistent results. The effect of ambient temperature on very early, early, or late PTB may also be different. Several studies stratified the associations by the timing of PTB and yielded incongruent results [ 5 , 6 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 18 , 23 , 24 ]. However, stratifying by gestational age groups may induce a collider bias [ 33 ] and an alternative methodological approach may be pursued.

In this study, we aimed to examine the critical temperature exposure periods for PTB by using DLNMs and survival analysis in an innovative methodological approach. This enabled us to differentiate between PTB during various phases of pregnancy, estimate associations with realistic exposure scenarios throughout pregnancy, and examine vulnerable groups in Southern Israel by using a historical cohort of ∼130 000 births.
### Study design and study population

We employed a historical cohort design utilizing electronic health records of members of Clalit Health Services (henceforth: Clalit), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, who gave birth at Soroka University Medical Centre in Be’er Sheva. Soroka is the only tertiary-level hospital in Southern Israel and ∼70% of the population in that area are Clalit members [ 34 ]. We obtained data on all live births that occurred at Soroka between 1 January 2005 and 31 December 2019 ( n =
 157 478) and had 131 599 births available for analysis after exclusions (see Supplementary Figure S1 for a complete description of the exclusions).

### Outcome definition

Gestational age at delivery was estimated at the hospital by using the last menstrual period (LMP) date (when available) and ultrasonography. PTB was defined as a birth occurring before 37 completed gestation weeks and categorized into four groups: <28, 28–31, 32–33, and 34–36 completed weeks [ 1 , 35 ].

### Exposure assessment

We assessed ambient temperature with a spatiotemporal model—an ensemble of machine-learning models of random forest, extreme gradient boosting, and generalized additive models [ 36 ]. Its estimates are based on satellite measurements, observations from weather stations, and reanalysis of synoptic conditions. The model performs well with an overall root mean square error of 0.3°C, providing hourly temperature estimates for a grid of 1 km × 1 km for Israel for the study period [ 36 ].

The Clalit database provided coordinates for residential addresses when available. As noted above, we excluded all addresses outside the southern district ( n =
 3558; 2.4%), as they might have been outdated. For other addresses, the geocoding quality and exposure assignment are described in Supplementary Table S1 . Further details on the exposure assessment are found in the Supplementary Material .

### Covariates

We drew a directed acyclic graph (DAG) [ 37 ] showing our assumptions about the causal relationships among the study variables to determine the minimal set of variables to be conditioned to eliminate bias and confounding ( Fig. 1a ). According to the analysis of the DAG using DAGitty [ 38 ], the minimal set of variables to be adjusted for was: SES, ethnicity, locality, seasonality, and air pollution ( Fig. 1b ). As the confounding effects of air pollution and locality on other associations of temperature and pregnancy outcomes in the region seemed negligible in prior studies, we adjusted for these variables only in sensitivity analyses.

We examined effect modification by ethnicity (Arab/Jewish), infant sex, area-level SES, and pre-pregnancy BMI. Area-level SES was based on census-level small-statistical-area classification from the Israel Central Bureau of Statistics [ 39 ]. We estimated pre-pregnancy BMI by the median of height measurements and the last weight measurement within 2 years prior to the pregnancy until the first month of the pregnancy.

### Statistical analyses

We fitted Cox proportional-hazards models with time-dependent covariates integrated with a DLNM [ 28 , 40 ]. We utilized gestation weeks as the time and birth as the event to estimate how the conditional associations between the mean weekly temperature and PTB varied throughout gestation. Further details about the model can be found in the Supplementary Material .

Formula 1 specifies the primary model equation for the hazard function λ i ( t ) ⁠ , where C i represents time-independent covariates, such as SES and ethnicity, Z i ( t ) represents time-dependent covariates (sine and cosine of the week of the year for each gestation week, adjusting for seasonality), and X i represents the time-dependent exposures (i.e. weekly temperature) added into the model in a cross-basis function s x ( X i , t ; β x ) ⁠ . λ 0 ( t ) is the baseline hazard function and β c ⁠ , β z ⁠ , and β x are the other Cox model parameters with respect to the time-independent covariates C i ⁠ , time-dependent covariates Z i ( t ) ⁠ , and the cross-basis functions, respectively [ 41 ]. The causal structure assumed for the time-dependent covariates and exposures is demonstrated by the schematic DAG in Supplementary Figure S2 . Robust standard errors were used to account for the dependency between pregnancies of the same mother [ 42 ].

To examine whether the association of exposure in a specific gestation week with PTB changes for different delivery weeks, we used an extension of the previous Cox model, which enables time-dependent coefficients differing by PTB groups based on gestational age at delivery (as defined above) without stratifying the model (see Supplementary Material for technical details) [ 40 ].

In addition, we used the primary model to examine the associations of exposure to minimum (instead of mean) temperature with the risk of PTB. We also added possible effect modifiers to the primary models as interaction terms, calculated P -values for interaction using likelihood ratio tests, and stratified models by these modifiers. In sensitivity analyses, we further adjusted our models for air pollution by using weekly PM 2.5 concentrations and locality. We also fitted a model without seasonality covariates. All analyses were performed in R, version 4.3.1 [ 43 ], using the survival [ 42 ] and dlnm [ 28 ] packages.

### Risk estimation by temperature trajectories

To demonstrate the implications of our results for the risk of PTB by different realistic exposure trajectories throughout pregnancy, we estimated the survival probability by Week 37: S ( t = 37 ) ⁠ . For this estimation, we used 37 weeks of exposure and covariates of each pregnancy according to LMP date and residential address, regardless of the actual date of birth. We then estimated the cumulative PTB risk by using 1 – S ( t = 37 ) ⁠ , i.e. the probability of not completing 37 gestational weeks.

For the current dataset, the seasonal factor plays a major role in determining the exposure estimated by the spatiotemporal model: by using a univariate linear regression model, we found that 86% of the variability in weekly temperature can be explained by the LMP month. Therefore, we calculated the average estimated PTB risk by using the LMP month. Finally, we estimated the relative risks for each LMP month by dividing the average risk in each month by the risk of the lowest average risk (March). The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated by bootstrapping using 500 samples with replacement. A formal description of this approach can be found in the Supplementary Material .
In our cohort of 131 599 deliveries in Southern Israel, the prevalence of PTB was 7%. More than half of the study population were Bedouin-Arab and nearly half of the mothers with available pre-pregnancy BMI data were overweight or obese ( Table 1 ). Supplementary Figure S3 illustrates the exposure distribution, Supplementary Figure S4 presents its spatial distribution, and Supplementary Figure S5 demonstrates the correlation structure among exposure weeks of gestation. The proportions of Arabs and mothers with lower SES were higher in the lower-temperature quintiles ( Supplementary Table S2 ) and Arabs comprised the majority in the first and second SES quartiles ( Supplementary Table S3 ).

Temperature exposures in gestation Weeks 1–28 were not associated with PTB. However, higher temperatures during the third trimester were associated with a higher risk of early delivery. For example, exposure to 31°C (99th percentile) in Week 29 presented an hazard ratio (HR) of 1.02 (95% CI: 1.00–1.03) with PTB compared with the minimum-risk temperature (16°C). Similarly, exposures to 31°C in Weeks 30–37 were associated with PTB, with increasing strength towards the end of the third trimester. The strongest association was for exposure during Week 37 (HR= 1.04, 95% CI: 1.01–1.07; Fig. 2 ). There were no major differences in associations by groups of PTB severity ( Supplementary Figures S6–S9 ).

We did not find any interaction with ethnicity and SES ( P for interaction = 0.18 and 0.84, respectively). Weekly associations were slightly stronger in female than male fetuses ( P for interaction < 0.001; Supplementary Figure S10 ). In addition, associations were somewhat different in women with pre-pregnancy underweight or overweight, but the pattern of difference was unclear ( P for interaction <0.001; Supplementary Figure S11 ). Cancelling the seasonality adjustment or adding adjustments for PM 2.5 and locality did not materially change the results ( Supplementary Figures S12–S14 ). Associations with minimum (instead of mean) daily temperature were also similar ( Supplementary Figure S15 ).

The average estimated risk of PTB across exposure trajectories defined by the LMP month displayed a clear seasonal pattern, with the lowest risk estimated for pregnancies with LMP between February and April and the highest risk for those with LMP during the autumn ( Fig. 3 , top). The average estimated risk by LMP month varied between 6.5% and 7.6% for pregnancies with LMP in March and October, respectively, translated into a relative risk of 1.17 with a 95% CI of 1.07–1.27 ( Fig. 3 , middle; Supplementary Table S4 ). Exposure trajectories for pregnancies starting in the autumn also included the highest temperatures during Weeks 33–37 of gestation ( Fig. 3 , bottom).
The Soroka Institutional Review Board approved the study (approval number: 0341-19), including the exemption from informed consent due to the sample size and de-identified nature of the records.
question: Based on the study's analysis of temperature exposure during pregnancy and its impact on infant delivery occurring before 37 weeks of completed gestation, associated with high neonatal mortality and significant morbidity, with significant neonatal mortality and morbidity consequences, what can be inferred about the relationship between cumulative exposure patterns and observed risk differences across pregnancy timing?

choices.Option: The lack of interaction with ethnicity and SES suggests that environmental temperature has an equal impact across all socioeconomic and ethnic groups in Southern Israel.
The hazard ratios reported for weekly temperature exposure in the third trimester are sufficient to conclude that heat exposure during Week 37 causes a 4% increase in preterm birth risk.
The methodological innovation of using LMP month to define exposure trajectories allows for precise identification of the exact gestational week when temperature exposure is most harmful.

Pregnancies starting in the autumn were exposed to the highest temperatures in Weeks 33–37 and had the highest estimated PTB risk, suggesting that seasonal temperature patterns directly determine preterm birth outcomes.

The cumulative associations of temperature exposure throughout pregnancy, when comparing pregnancies by month of last menstrual period, are approximately 4-fold higher than the weekly associations reported as hazard ratios.

Congenital anomalies (CAs), also known as congenital malformations or birth defects, are structural or functional anomalies that occur in utero . They may be identifiable prenatally, at birth, during infancy, or later in life. Globally, an estimated 240 000 newborns die annually within 28 days of birth due to congenital disorders, and 170 000 additional related deaths occur up to 5 years of age [ 1 ].

In recent decades, deaths from communicable diseases in both high- and low-income countries have decreased [ 2 ]. Consequently, the relative contribution of CAs to under-five mortality is now among the 10 leading causes of death worldwide [ 3 , 4 ].

For many CAs, including rare structural anomalies, most deaths occur in the first weeks of life, and survival beyond 10 years, conditional on surviving this crucial window, is actually quite high, frequently over 90% [ 5 ]. Children with cardiovascular, renal, and gastrointestinal abnormalities require specialized care. However, there is little population-based research about the long-term survival of individuals with a broad range of CAs beyond the second decade of life [ 3 ]. Information about the long-term outcomes of individuals with CAs who reach adulthood is important for counselling affected individuals and their parents and for adequate planning of health and other services [ 3 ].

We aimed to investigate associations between CAs and premature adult mortality. We focused on individuals who survived to the age of 18 years, comparing all-cause adult mortality of individuals with and without CAs in the Jerusalem Perinatal Study (JPS), a birth cohort with over four decades of follow-up. Previous work from this cohort had demonstrated a relatively high rate of CAs and an association between consanguinity and CAs [ 6 , 7 ].
### Study design and study population

The population-based JPS cohort has been previously described [ 8 ]. It includes all 92 408 still- and live births to West Jerusalem mothers in 1964–76. Vital status was verified via linkage of unique national identity numbers to the Israeli Population Registry, updated through 31 December 2016. Data on demographic, perinatal, and parental characteristics were obtained at birth. We excluded stillbirths ( n = 949), offspring who could not be traced in the Population Registry ( n = 1409; henceforth “unverified”), and those who did not survive until 18 years of age ( n = 2429). The final study population consisted of 87 621 individuals ( Fig. 1 ).

### Study variables

The outcome variable was all-cause adult mortality, defined as deaths occurring at 18 years or older. Data on CAs and affected body systems were recorded postnatally using birth records, and updated during follow-up in the first months of life from hospitalization records, nurse examinations, and death certificates [ 6 ]. Prenatal ultrasound was not prevalent during this period. Starting in 1969 CAs were categorized in terms of severity according to the International Classification of Diseases (Seventh Edition), in use at the time [ 7 ]. Of 5538 individuals with missing CA status at birth, 5078 (92%) were defined as CA-free using data collected during postnatal follow-up ( Supplementary Methods ). However, the affected body system remained missing for 36% of infants with CAs.

We defined four exposures of interest: dichotomous CA status (none versus at least one), multiplicity (0 = none, 1 = single, and 2 = multiple anomalies), severity (0 = none, 1 = only mild/moderate anomaly, 2 = only severe anomaly, and 3 = moderate and severe anomalies combined). Finally, we assessed CAs in specific body systems, namely the cardiovascular, central nervous system (CNS), gastrointestinal, respiratory, genitourinary and musculoskeletal systems, ear or eye, other (unclassified), or “unknown” system. Risk of death was assessed separately by each system.

All multivariable models were adjusted for the following covariates: Offspring sex, birth weight in gram (<2500, 2500–4000, and >4000), mode of delivery (vaginal/caesarean section), maternal place of birth (Israel or abroad), maternal age at delivery (<20, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35+), maternal level of education at delivery (0–8, 9–12, and >12 years) and socioeconomic status recoded into three levels (low, medium, high) [ 8 ]. Participants with missing values for maternal age (0.7%), education (6.7%), and delivery mode (2.8%) were assigned a separate “missing” category and therefore retained in the multivariable analyses.

### Statistical analysis

We plotted crude survival probabilities from birth for the entire cohort by presence of CA and CAs in specific body systems ( n = 90 050), using the Kaplan–Meier approach and counting time from birth to death or end of follow-up (31 December 2016).

All subsequent analyses were based on the subsample of individuals who survived to 18 years of age ( n = 87 621). In multivariate models, time-to-event was defined from the 18th birthday to death or censored at the end of follow-up. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated by fitting Cox proportional hazard models. We also present adjusted absolute risks (1 − survival probability) and risk differences for individuals with and without CAs.

Separate models were constructed using the following exposures: CA status, number of CAs, anomaly severity, compared to a reference category of no CAs. Additional models compared mortality risks by the presence of a CA in a specific body system to “No CAs” or CAs in other systems. The models were adjusted for covariates previously found to be related to CA or death [ 9 , 10 ] and those found to be associated with mortality in univariate Cox models (not shown).

We conducted several sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Materials ): first, we assessed the impact of excluding “unverified” individuals by predicting their absolute risks over time from the CA status-mortality model using their baseline characteristics. We next compared these with observed risks in verified individuals using the Kaplan–Meier approach. Next, to evaluate the potential bias due to missing CA data in a few specific birth hospitals, we excluded infants born in these hospitals and compared results with the main models.

Thirdly, we imputed missing values in maternal age, education, and delivery mode using the multiple imputations by chained equations with five imputation datasets (R package mice ) [ 11 ]. The missing-at-random assumption was tested and supported by strong associations between the probability of missingness in imputed variables and the observed predictors.

To verify that our findings were robust to the non-independence of sibling observations, we conducted analyses selecting a single random child per family . Finally, since our data on family background are limited, we performed a sibling fixed-effects analysis. This design compares the mortality of siblings with and without anomalies within the same family and thus controls for unmeasured shared factors, including genetic background and household environment, that might confound the observed association.

For all main Cox models, the proportional hazards assumption was examined using the test of scaled Schoenfeld’s residuals [ 12 ] (R package survival [ 13 ]). Subsequently, we stratified all the main models on offspring’s sex and maternal education, which were the only variables exhibiting time-dependency ( Supplementary Tables S16–S19h and Figs S5–S8h ). The analyses were performed in R software (version 4.2.2).
The final study population is shown in Fig. 1 . Of the 92 408 offspring in the JPS cohort, 91 459 (99%) were live births, of which 90 050 (97.5%) were verified in the Population Registry. Kaplan–Meier plots illustrate mortality over the life-course ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ) for this population; most infants with malformations in cardiovascular and CNSs died very soon after birth and well before reaching 18 years. Of the verified population, 87 621 (97.3%) individuals attained the age of 18 years (and are the focus of this report), of whom 5621 (6.4%) had some form of CA.

Follow-up time from the 18th birthday ranged from 0 to 35 years with a median of 27.5 years and totalled 2 428 002.5 person-years. Deaths occurred in 1454 individuals from age 18.0 to 52.6 years; of these, 143 (2.5%) were in individuals with and 1311 (1.6%) without CAs ( Fig. 1 ).

Individuals with anomalies who survived to age 18 years were more likely to be male, to have low or high birth weight, low socioeconomic status at birth, Israel-born mothers, and to be delivered by caesarean section compared to those without CAs. Maternal age and education level at the time of delivery were similar between the groups ( Table 1 ), as was paternal age (mean 32 years ±7 in both). Of 5228 mothers whose children had CAs, about 7% ( n = 365) had more than one affected child.

In a multivariable Cox model, having any CA was associated with a 53% increase in the risk of death (CI: 1.29–1.83, P < .001) after stratification by offspring sex and maternal education and adjusting for other covariates ( Table 2 ).

Similar increased risks were observed for participants with single malformations (HR = 1.51, CI: 1.27–1.81) compared to those with none ( Table 3 ). The presence of multiple anomalies was associated with an even higher mortality risk (HR = 1.99, CI: 0.99–3.99), although the CI crossed unity. The risk of adult mortality was doubled in persons with severe anomalies (HR = 2.21, CI: 1.75–2.77) and with combined moderate and severe CAs (HR = 2.19, CI: 1.09–4.40) compared with those without anomalies. There was, however, no association between having a moderate anomaly and adult mortality. Adjusted HRs were elevated for CAs in the cardiovascular (HR = 4.81, CI: 2.15–10.70), gastrointestinal (HR = 2.74, CI: 1.47–5.11), and genitourinary (HR = 1.51, CI: 1.07–2.14) systems and among individuals with a CA in an unknown system (HR = 1.42, CI: 1.09–1.86) compared to all the others.

The absolute risk of death varied over time, and after 30 years of follow-up was 2.4% (CI: 1.8%–3.0%) in those with CAs, but only 1.5% (CI: 1.2%–1.9%) in those without, resulting in a risk difference of 0.9 percentage points ( Supplementary Figs S2 and S3 and Table S4 ).

All analyses aimed to assess the robustness of our findings produced results consistent with the main models. Supplementary Fig. S4 shows that the predicted risks for unverified individuals were almost identical to those of the verified cohort members in both exposure groups, suggesting that their risk of death is similar. The imputation analysis confirmed that missingness in covariates was unlikely to affect our results ( Supplementary Tables S6–S8 ). Likewise, the analyses excluding offspring born in hospitals with 75% of the missing CA status also supported our main estimates ( Supplementary Tables S9 and S10 ). Additionally, selecting a single random child per family suggested that non-independence of observations did not bias the reported associations ( Supplementary Tables S11–S13 ).

Finally, the fixed-effect within-family models were also consistent with the main analysis: siblings with CA, with all other shared characteristics being equal, had a 1.6-fold higher risk of adult mortality (CI: 1.06–2.42, Supplementary Table S14 ), and system-specific assessments, where there were sufficient cases to assess these, were generally consistent with the original models ( Supplementary Table S15 ).
The study was approved by the institutional review board (Helsinki committee) at Hadassah University Hospital (HMO0200-09). Since anonymized retrospective data were used, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived.
question: What can be inferred about the long-term health outcomes of individuals who survive infancy with structural or functional defects present at birth with prenatal origin that may lead to physical or developmental disabilities, based on repeated measurements over extended periods on individuals with a shared prenatal origin of birth defects to track incidence and risk of health outcomes?

choices.Option: Individuals with congenital anomalies who survive infancy are at a significantly lower risk of chronic disease in adulthood compared to those without anomalies, due to early medical interventions.

The increased risk of premature adult mortality in individuals with congenital anomalies may be primarily due to the long-term effects of prenatal ultrasound exposure and diagnostic radiation during infancy.

The presence of congenital anomalies, particularly in the cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary systems, is associated with an increased risk of premature adult mortality, even after surviving to age 18.
The long-term survival of individuals with congenital anomalies beyond 10 years is primarily due to the widespread use of prenatal ultrasound and early surgical correction in the 1960s and 1970s.
The high rate of consanguinity in the Jerusalem Perinatal Study cohort explains the majority of the observed association between congenital anomalies and premature adult mortality.
